topic: Proper Subsets of a Finite Set
questionText: If a finite set A contains 5 distinct elements, how many proper subsets does A possess?
explanation: A set with n = 5 elements has 2⁵ = 32 total subsets in its power set; excluding the set A itself leaves 2⁵ − 1 = 31 proper subsets.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Sets and Relations

topic: Number of Relations Between Two Sets
questionText: If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 2, what is the total number of distinct relations that can be defined from set A to set B?
explanation: The Cartesian product A × B contains 3 × 2 = 6 ordered pairs; every subset of A × B is a relation from A to B, giving 2⁶ = 64 distinct relations.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Sets and Relations

questionText: In a retail payment survey of 120 shoppers, 72 use UPI apps, 54 use Credit Cards, and 18 pay exclusively in cash (using neither UPI nor Credit Cards). How many shoppers use BOTH UPI apps and Credit Cards?
explanation: n(U ∪ C) = 120 − 18 = 102. By inclusion-exclusion, n(U ∩ C) = n(U) + n(C) − n(U ∪ C) = 72 + 54 − 102 = 24.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Sets and Relations

questionText: On the set Z of all integers, consider the relation R = {(a, b) ∈ Z × Z : (a − b) is divisible by 5}. Which properties does R satisfy?

options.text: Reflexive and Symmetric, but NOT Transitive
Symmetric and Transitive, but NOT Reflexive
Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive (an Equivalence Relation)

explanation: a − a = 0 is divisible by 5 (reflexive); if 5 | (a − b) then 5 | (b − a) (symmetric); if 5 | (a − b) and 5 | (b − c) then 5 | (a − c) (transitive). Hence R is an Equivalence Relation.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Sets and Relations

questionText: Among 200 Commerce students, 110 read Economic Times (E), 90 read Business Standard (B), and 75 read Mint (M); 45 read both E & B, 35 read both B & M, 30 read both E & M, and 15 read all three dailies. How many students read EXACTLY ONE of the three financial newspapers?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Sets and Relations

topic: Range of a Relation Over Natural Numbers
questionText: A relation R on the set of natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...} is defined by R = {(x, y) : x, y ∈ N and 2x + y = 11}. What is the sum of all elements in the Range of R?
explanation: For x ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, y = 11 − 2x takes natural values {9, 7, 5, 3, 1} (for x ≥ 6, y ≤ −1 ∉ N). Sum of elements in Range(R) = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Sets and Relations

questionText: If f(x) = 3x² − 5x + 4, find the value of f(2) + f(−1).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Functions

questionText: What is the largest subset of R (real numbers) that forms the domain of f(x) = 1 / √(9 − x²)?
explanation: For 1 / √(9 − x²) to be a finite real number, the radicand in the denominator must be strictly positive: 9 − x² > 0 ⇒ x² < 9 ⇒ x ∈ (−3, 3).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Functions

topic: Break-Even Analysis Using Cost and Revenue Functions
questionText: A small manufacturing firm has monthly fixed costs of ₹36,000, variable production cost of ₹140 per unit, and sells each unit at ₹230. Find the break-even output level x where Total Revenue equals Total Cost.
explanation: Total Cost C(x) = 36,000 + 140x and Total Revenue R(x) = 230x. At break-even, 230x = 36,000 + 140x ⇒ 90x = 36,000 ⇒ x = 400 units.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Functions

questionText: If f(x) = (4x + 3) / (5x − 4) for x ≠ 4/5, what is the value of the composite expression (f ∘ f)(7)?
explanation: f(7) = (28 + 3) / (35 − 4) = 31 / 31 = 1, and f(f(7)) = f(1) = (4 + 3) / (5 − 4) = 7 (since f is a self-inverse function satisfying f(f(x)) = x).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Functions

topic: Recovering a Function from Function Composition
questionText: Let f : R → R be defined by f(x) = 2x + 5, and suppose a function g : R → R satisfies (g ∘ f)(x) = 4x² + 20x + 19 for all x ∈ R. Find the value of g(3).
explanation: To find g(3), set f(x) = 2x + 5 = 3 ⇒ x = −1. Substituting x = −1 into g(f(x)) = 4x² + 20x + 19 gives g(3) = 4(1) − 20 + 19 = 3 (equivalently g(t) = t² − 6).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Functions

topic: Modulus and Conjugate of a Complex Number
questionText: For the complex number z = 5 − 12i, what are its modulus |z| and complex conjugate z̄ respectively?
explanation: |z| = √(5² + (−12)²) = √(25 + 144) = 13, and changing the sign of the imaginary part yields z̄ = 5 + 12i.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Complex Numbers

topic: Integral Powers of Imaginary Unit i
questionText: Simplify the complex sum: i⁴⁹ + i⁵⁰ + i⁵¹ + i⁵² + i⁵³ (where i = √−1).
explanation: Any four consecutive integer powers of i sum to zero (i⁵⁰ + i⁵¹ + i⁵² + i⁵³ = 0), leaving i⁴⁹ = i^(4×12 + 1) = i.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Complex Numbers

topic: Division of Complex Numbers in a + bi Form
questionText: Express (13 + 13i) / (2 + 3i) in the standard form a + bi, where a, b ∈ R.
explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by (2 − 3i): 13(1 + i)(2 − 3i) / (4 + 9) = (1 + i)(2 − 3i) = 2 − 3i + 2i − 3i² = 5 − i.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Complex Numbers

topic: Algebra of Complex Cube Roots of Unity
questionText: If ω is a non-real complex cube root of unity (ω³ = 1, 1 + ω + ω² = 0), evaluate the product (2 − ω)(2 − ω²)(2 − ω¹⁰)(2 − ω¹¹).
explanation: Since ω¹⁰ = ω and ω¹¹ = ω², the expression equals [(2 − ω)(2 − ω²)]². Expanding (2 − ω)(2 − ω²) = 4 − 2(ω + ω²) + ω³ = 4 − 2(−1) + 1 = 7, so 7² = 49.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Complex Numbers

topic: Solving Simultaneous Real Unknowns in a Complex Equation
questionText: If real numbers x and y satisfy [x / (1 + i)] + [y / (1 − 2i)] = 3, find the value of (x + y).
explanation: Rationalising denominators: x(1 − i)/2 + y(1 + 2i)/5 = 3 ⇒ (5x + 2y) + i(−5x + 4y) = 30 + 0i. Equating imaginary part to 0 gives 5x = 4y; substituting into 5x + 2y = 30 gives 6y = 30 ⇒ y = 5, x = 4, so x + y = 9.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Complex Numbers

topic: General Term of a Geometric Progression
questionText: Find the 8th term of the Geometric Progression: 3, 6, 12, 24, ...
explanation: Here first term a = 3 and common ratio r = 2; T₈ = a·r⁷ = 3 × 2⁷ = 3 × 128 = 384.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Sequences and Series

topic: Relation Among AM, GM, and HM
questionText: If the Arithmetic Mean (AM) of two positive numbers is 16 and their Harmonic Mean (HM) is 9, what is their Geometric Mean (GM)?
explanation: For any two positive numbers, GM² = AM × HM = 16 × 9 = 144, so GM = 12.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Sequences and Series

topic: Sum to Infinity of a Convergent G.P.
questionText: Find the sum to infinity of the Geometric Series: 12 + 8 + 16/3 + 32/9 + ...
explanation: First term a = 12 and common ratio r = 8/12 = 2/3 (|r| < 1). Sum to infinity S∞ = a / (1 − r) = 12 / (1 − 2/3) = 36.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Sequences and Series

questionText: Evaluate the finite series sum: Σ (from r = 1 to 10) of (3r² − 2r).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Sequences and Series

topic: Three Terms in G.P. from Sum and Product
questionText: Three positive numbers are in Geometric Progression such that their sum is 26 and their product is 216. What is the largest of the three numbers?
explanation: Let the numbers be a/r, a, ar. Their product a³ = 216 ⇒ a = 6. Sum: 6/r + 6 + 6r = 26 ⇒ 3r² − 10r + 3 = 0 ⇒ r = 3 or 1/3, giving the numbers 2, 6, 18; the largest is 18.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Sequences and Series

questionText: What is the exact sum of the first n terms of the series 5 + 55 + 555 + ...?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Sequences and Series

topic: Slope and Y-Intercept of a Line
questionText: Find the slope and y-intercept of the straight line 3x − 4y + 12 = 0.
explanation: Rewriting in slope-intercept form y = mx + c: 4y = 3x + 12 ⇒ y = (3/4)x + 3, giving slope m = 3/4 and y-intercept c = 3.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Locus and Straight Line

questionText: Find the equation of the straight line passing through the point (2, −3) and perpendicular to the line 4x + 3y − 7 = 0.
explanation: Slope of 4x + 3y − 7 = 0 is −4/3, so the perpendicular slope is 3/4. Using point-slope form: y − (−3) = (3/4)(x − 2) ⇒ 4y + 12 = 3x − 6 ⇒ 3x − 4y − 18 = 0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Locus and Straight Line

topic: Perpendicular Distance from a Point to a Line
questionText: What is the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point (3, −1) to the straight line 5x − 12y + 12 = 0?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Locus and Straight Line

topic: Equation of Locus from Difference of Squared Distances
questionText: Find the equation of the locus of a moving point P(x, y) given A(2, 3) and B(−1, 4) such that PA² − PB² = 14.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Locus and Straight Line

questionText: A straight line meets the X-axis at A and the Y-axis at B such that the segment AB intercepted between the axes is bisected at the point M(3, 4). What is the equation of the line?
explanation: Let A = (a, 0) and B = (0, b). Since M(3, 4) is the midpoint of AB, a/2 = 3 ⇒ a = 6 and b/2 = 4 ⇒ b = 8. By double-intercept form: x/6 + y/8 = 1 ⇒ 4x + 3y = 24.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Locus and Straight Line

questionText: For what value of x is the 2 × 2 matrix A = [[x + 1, 6], [2, 4]] a singular matrix?
explanation: A square matrix is singular iff det(A) = 0: 4(x + 1) − (6 × 2) = 0 ⇒ 4x + 4 = 12 ⇒ x = 2.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Determinants and Matrices

questionText: If A = [a_ij] is a real skew-symmetric square matrix (so that Aᵀ = −A), what must be the value of every principal diagonal element a_ii?
explanation: For diagonal entries (i = j), skew-symmetry requires a_ii = −a_ii ⇒ 2a_ii = 0 ⇒ a_ii = 0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Determinants and Matrices

questionText: Evaluate the 3 × 3 determinant with rows: Row 1 = (2, −1, 3), Row 2 = (1, 4, −2), Row 3 = (3, 1, 5).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Determinants and Matrices

questionText: Outlet P sold 10 shirts, 8 trousers, and 5 jackets; Outlet Q sold 12 shirts, 6 trousers, and 4 jackets. Unit selling prices are ₹800, ₹1,200, and ₹2,000 respectively. Using matrix multiplication (Quantity Matrix × Price Column Vector), find total sales revenues of Outlets P and Q.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Determinants and Matrices

questionText: Solving the linear system 2x + 3y = 13 and 5x − 2y = 4 by Cramer's Rule, find the determinants D, D_y, and the solution value of y.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Determinants and Matrices

questionText: Given the 2 × 2 matrix A = [[3, 1], [−1, 2]] and identity matrix I₂ = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], find the scalar k such that A² − 5A + kI₂ = O (the null matrix).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Determinants and Matrices

questionText: Evaluate lim (x → 3) of (x⁴ − 81) / (x − 3).
explanation: Using lim (x → a) (xⁿ − aⁿ) / (x − a) = n·a^(n−1): for n = 4 and a = 3, the limit equals 4 × 3³ = 4 × 27 = 108.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Limits

questionText: What is the exact value of lim (x → 0) of (5ˣ − 1) / x?
explanation: By the standard exponential limit formula, lim (x → 0) (aˣ − 1) / x = logₑ a (for a > 0), giving logₑ 5.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Limits

questionText: Evaluate lim (x → 0) of [√(4 + x) − 2] / x.
explanation: Multiplying numerator and denominator by [√(4 + x) + 2] yields [(4 + x) − 4] / [x(√(4 + x) + 2)] = 1 / [√(4 + x) + 2] → 1 / (2 + 2) = 1/4.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Limits

questionText: Evaluate lim (x → 0) of (e^(5x) − e^(2x)) / x.
explanation: Rewriting as [(e^(5x) − 1)/x] − [(e^(2x) − 1)/x] and applying lim (t → 0) (eᵗ − 1)/t = 1 gives 5(1) − 2(1) = 3.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Limits

questionText: Evaluate lim (x → 2) of (x³ − 7x + 6) / (x² + x − 6).
explanation: Factorising numerator: x³ − 7x + 6 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x − 3) = (x − 2)(x − 1)(x + 3). Factorising denominator: x² + x − 6 = (x − 2)(x + 3). Cancelling for x ≠ 2 leaves lim (x → 2) (x − 1) = 1.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Limits

topic: Definition of Continuity at a Point
questionText: Under what condition is a real-valued function f(x) continuous at x = a in its domain?

options.text: lim (x → a⁻) f(x) = lim (x → a⁺) f(x) = f(a) (finite)
f(x) is defined only for integers
f(a) = 0 regardless of left-hand and right-hand limits
lim (x → a⁻) f(x) ≠ lim (x → a⁺) f(x)

explanation: Continuity at x = a requires that f(a) exists, the two-sided limit lim (x → a) f(x) exists finitely (LHL = RHL), and both equal f(a).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Continuity

questionText: If f(x) = (x² − 25) / (x − 5) for x ≠ 5 and f(5) = k is continuous at x = 5, find k.
explanation: For continuity at x = 5, k = f(5) = lim (x → 5) [(x − 5)(x + 5) / (x − 5)] = lim (x → 5) (x + 5) = 10.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Continuity

questionText: If f(x) = logₑ(1 + 6x) / (2x) for x ≠ 0 is continuous at x = 0, what must be the value of f(0)?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Continuity

questionText: A piecewise function is defined by: f(x) = 3x + 2 for x < 1; f(x) = ax + b for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3; and f(x) = x² + 8 for x > 3. If f(x) is continuous throughout R, find the constants a and b.
explanation: Continuity at x = 1 gives a(1) + b = 3(1) + 2 = 5 ⇒ a + b = 5. Continuity at x = 3 gives 3a + b = 3² + 8 = 17. Subtracting yields 2a = 12 ⇒ a = 6 and b = −1.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Continuity

questionText: Consider f(x) = |x − 4| / (x − 4) for x ≠ 4, and f(4) = 0. How is the behaviour of f(x) at x = 4 classified?

options.text: Removable discontinuity that can be cured by setting f(4) = 1
Irremovable (jump) discontinuity because LHL = −1 while RHL = +1

explanation: For x < 4, |x − 4| = −(x − 4) so LHL = −1; for x > 4, |x − 4| = x − 4 so RHL = +1. Since LHL ≠ RHL, lim (x → 4) f(x) does not exist—an irremovable jump discontinuity.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Continuity

questionText: Differentiate y = x⁴ − 6eˣ + 8 logₑ x − 15 with respect to x (for x > 0).
explanation: Applying standard derivatives term-by-term: d/dx(x⁴) = 4x³, d/dx(−6eˣ) = −6eˣ, d/dx(8 logₑ x) = 8/x, and d/dx(−15) = 0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Differentiation

questionText: In commercial applications of calculus, if C = f(x) represents Total Cost of producing x units, what economic concept is measured by the first derivative dC/dx?
explanation: Marginal Cost is the instantaneous rate of change of Total Cost with respect to output x, given in calculus by MC = dC/dx.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Differentiation

questionText: If y = x²·eˣ, find the value of dy/dx at x = 1.
explanation: By the product rule, dy/dx = x²·eˣ + 2x·eˣ = (x² + 2x)eˣ. Evaluating at x = 1 gives (1 + 2)e¹ = 3e.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Differentiation

questionText: If f(x) = (3x + 2) / (2x − 1) for x ≠ 1/2, calculate f′(2).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Differentiation

topic: Output Where Marginal Cost Equals Average Cost
questionText: A manufacturer's Total Cost function (in ₹) for x units is C(x) = 2x² + 30x + 800 (x > 0). Find the output level x at which Marginal Cost (MC) equals Average Cost (AC).
explanation: MC = dC/dx = 4x + 30, and AC = C(x)/x = 2x + 30 + 800/x. Setting MC = AC gives 4x + 30 = 2x + 30 + 800/x ⇒ 2x = 800/x ⇒ x² = 400 ⇒ x = 20 units (where AC is minimised at ₹110).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Differentiation

topic: Demand Law and Marginal Revenue Zero Output
questionText: The price-demand relation for a firm's product is p = 120 − 3x, where p is unit price (₹) and x is quantity demanded. Find (i) Marginal Revenue at x = 15 units and (ii) the output x at which Marginal Revenue becomes zero.

options.text: MR at x = 15 is ₹75; MR becomes zero at x = 40 units
MR at x = 15 is ₹30; MR becomes zero at x = 40 units
MR at x = 15 is ₹30; MR becomes zero at x = 20 units
MR at x = 15 is ₹45; MR becomes zero at x = 25 units

explanation: Total Revenue R(x) = p·x = 120x − 3x², so Marginal Revenue MR = dR/dx = 120 − 6x. At x = 15, MR = 120 − 90 = ₹30; setting 120 − 6x = 0 gives x = 20 units (revenue-maximising output).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Differentiation

questionText: Which statistical graph is specifically used to locate Quartiles, Deciles, and Percentiles graphically?
explanation: Partition values depend on cumulative frequencies (less-than or more-than ogives), whereas a Histogram is used graphically to locate the Mode.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Partition Values

questionText: For 11 sorted test scores—14, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36, 40, 44, 48—what are the First Quartile (Q1) and Second Quartile (Q2)?

questionText: Nine listed companies have Price-to-Earnings ratios: 15, 8, 28, 12, 20, 10, 32, 24, 18. Compute the inter-decile spread (D9 − D1).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Partition Values

questionText: Given values x = (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) with corresponding frequencies f = (3, 6, 8, 4, 2), compute P75.
explanation: Total N = 23 and cumulative frequencies (cf) are 3, 9, 17, 21, 23. P75 = size of 75(23 + 1)/100 = 18th observation; the first cf ≥ 18 is 21, corresponding to x = 20.

topic: Finding Two Missing Frequencies from Q2 and Total N
questionText: In the distribution 0–10 (f = 5), 10–20 (f = x), 20–30 (f = 20), 30–40 (f = 15), 40–50 (f = y), total frequency N = 60 and Second Quartile (Q2) = 28. Find x and y.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Partition Values

questionText: Six closing prices (in ₹) of a share during a week were: 180, 220, 150, 250, 195, 210. Find the Range and Coefficient of Range.
explanation: Largest value L = 250, Smallest value S = 150. Range = L − S = ₹100; Coefficient of Range = (250 − 150) / (250 + 150) = 100 / 400 = 0.25.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Measures of Dispersion

topic: Quartile Deviation and Coefficient of QD
questionText: If the First Quartile (Q1) of a wage distribution is ₹30 and the Third Quartile (Q3) is ₹50, find the Quartile Deviation (QD) and Coefficient of QD.
explanation: QD (Semi-interquartile range) = (Q3 − Q1)/2 = (50 − 30)/2 = ₹10; Coefficient of QD = (Q3 − Q1)/(Q3 + Q1) = 20/80 = 0.25.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Measures of Dispersion

topic: Variance and Standard Deviation of Ungrouped Data
questionText: Compute the population Variance (σ²) and Standard Deviation (σ) of the observations: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
explanation: Mean x̄ = 8; squared deviations from mean are (−4)² + (−2)² + 0² + 2² + 4² = 40. Variance σ² = 40 / 5 = 8, and σ = √8 = 2√2.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Measures of Dispersion

questionText: Equity Fund X has a mean annual return of 15% with standard deviation 3%; Equity Fund Y has a mean annual return of 20% with standard deviation 5%. Using Coefficient of Variation (CV), which fund is more consistent?

options.text: Fund X (CV = 5%) is less consistent than Fund Y (CV = 4%)
Fund Y (CV = 25%) is more consistent because its mean return is higher
Fund X (CV = 20%) is more consistent than Fund Y (CV = 25%)

explanation: CV = (σ / x̄) × 100. CV(X) = (3/15) × 100 = 20%; CV(Y) = (5/20) × 100 = 25%. Lower CV signifies smaller relative variability, so Fund X is more consistent.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Measures of Dispersion

topic: Effect of Change of Origin and Scale on Variance
questionText: A random dataset X has Mean = 12 and Variance = 5. If each observation is transformed according to Y = 3X − 7, what are the Mean and Variance of Y?

options.text: Mean of Y = 36 and Variance of Y = 45
Mean of Y = 29 and Variance of Y = 15
Mean of Y = 29 and Variance of Y = 38
Mean of Y = 29 and Variance of Y = 45

explanation: For Y = aX + b: Mean ȳ = a·x̄ + b = 3(12) − 7 = 29. Variance is invariant to shift of origin (−7) and scales by a²: Var(Y) = 3² × Var(X) = 9 × 5 = 45.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Measures of Dispersion

questionText: Branch 1 has 40 employees with mean daily incentive ₹45 and SD ₹4; Branch 2 has 60 employees with mean daily incentive ₹55 and SD ₹5. Compute the Combined Variance of all 100 employees.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 11: Measures of Dispersion

questionText: In a unimodal Positively Skewed frequency distribution (longer tail toward higher values on the right), what inequality relates Mean, Median, and Mode?
explanation: High right-tail outliers pull the arithmetic Mean furthest right, with Median in between and Mode at the peak on the left: Mean > Median > Mode.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Skewness

topic: Bounds of Bowley's Coefficient of Skewness
questionText: Within what closed numerical interval does Bowley's quartile-based Coefficient of Skewness (S_b) always lie?
explanation: Because Q1 ≤ Q2 ≤ Q3, |(Q3 − Q2) − (Q2 − Q1)| ≤ (Q3 − Q2) + (Q2 − Q1) = Q3 − Q1, bounding S_b strictly between −1 and +1.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Skewness

questionText: For a distribution with Mean = 64, Mode = 70, and Variance = 144, compute Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Skewness (S_k).
explanation: Standard Deviation σ = √144 = 12. Karl Pearson's S_k = (Mean − Mode) / σ = (64 − 70) / 12 = −6 / 12 = −0.5 (negatively skewed).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 12: Skewness

questionText: Compute Bowley's Coefficient of Skewness for a dataset having Q1 = 22, Median (Q2) = 30, and Q3 = 46.

topic: Degrees of Freedom in a Contingency Table
questionText: In a Karl Pearson Chi-Square test of independence on a contingency table having 4 rows and 3 columns, what are the degrees of freedom?
explanation: Degrees of freedom for an r × c contingency table = (r − 1)(c − 1) = (4 − 1)(3 − 1) = 3 × 2 = 6.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Bivariate Frequency Distribution and Chi-Square

questionText: In a contingency table of N = 200 customers cross-classified by Age Group and Payment Mode, Row 1 has marginal total 80 and Column 2 has marginal total 65. Under independence, what is the expected cell frequency E₁₂?
explanation: Expected frequency E_ij = (Row i Total × Column j Total) / N = (80 × 65) / 200 = 5,200 / 200 = 26.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Bivariate Frequency Distribution and Chi-Square

topic: Conditional Frequency Percentage from Bivariate Table
questionText: A 2 × 2 bivariate table of (X, Y) has cell frequencies: (X₁, Y₁) = 15, (X₁, Y₂) = 25, (X₂, Y₁) = 20, and (X₂, Y₂) = 40 (total N = 100). In the conditional distribution of Y given X = X₁, what percentage belongs to Y₂?
explanation: Marginal total for X = X₁ is 15 + 25 = 40. Within X = X₁, the conditional relative share of Y₂ is (25 / 40) × 100% = 62.5%.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Bivariate Frequency Distribution and Chi-Square

questionText: Compute Karl Pearson's Chi-Square statistic χ² = Σ[(O − E)² / E] for the observed 2 × 2 table (N = 100): Row 1 = (30, 20) and Row 2 = (10, 40).
explanation: Row totals are (50, 50) and column totals are (40, 60), so expected frequencies are Row 1 = (20, 30) and Row 2 = (20, 30). Since |O − E| = 10 in every cell, χ² = 100/20 + 100/30 + 100/20 + 100/30 = 10 + 20/3 = 50/3 ≈ 16.67.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Bivariate Frequency Distribution and Chi-Square

topic: Goodness-of-Fit Chi-Square for Uniform Weekday Demand
questionText: A store manager tests whether customer arrivals are uniform across 5 weekdays (expected E_i = 50/day out of 250 customers). Actual arrivals from Monday to Friday were 60, 45, 55, 40, and 50. Find the value of χ².
explanation: Squared deviations (O_i − 50)² are 10² + (−5)² + 5² + (−10)² + 0² = 100 + 25 + 25 + 100 + 0 = 250. Dividing by E = 50 gives χ² = 250 / 50 = 5.0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 13: Bivariate Frequency Distribution and Chi-Square

questionText: If all plotted points (x_i, y_i) in a scatter diagram lie exactly along a straight line sloping downward from left to right, what is the value of r?
explanation: Exact collinearity along a negatively sloped line represents perfect negative linear correlation, so r = −1.

topic: Sign Sensitivity of Correlation Under Linear Scaling
questionText: Given that Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient between X and Y is r(X, Y) = 0.80, find r(U, V) where U = 2X + 5 and V = −3Y + 10.
explanation: Correlation magnitude is invariant under linear change of origin and scale, but because the scale multipliers (+2 and −3) have opposite signs, the sign reverses: r(U, V) = −0.80.

questionText: If ⁿC₈ = ⁿC₆, find the value of n and ⁿC₂.
explanation: Since ⁿC_a = ⁿC_b (with a ≠ b) implies n = a + b = 8 + 6 = 14, we get ¹⁴C₂ = (14 × 13) / 2 = 91.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 15: Permutations and Combinations

questionText: How many distinct 8-letter arrangements can be formed using all letters of the word 'COMMERCE'?
explanation: 'COMMERCE' has 8 letters with C repeated twice, M repeated twice, and E repeated twice. Distinct permutations = 8! / (2! × 2! × 2!) = 40,320 / 8 = 5,040.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 15: Permutations and Combinations

questionText: How many 4-digit numbers strictly greater than 5,000 can be formed from the digits {2, 3, 5, 7, 8} if repetition of digits is NOT allowed?
explanation: To exceed 5,000, the thousands place can be chosen from {5, 7, 8} in 3 ways; the remaining 3 places are filled from the remaining 4 digits in ⁴P₃ = 24 ways. Total = 3 × 24 = 72.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 15: Permutations and Combinations

questionText: From 6 Chartered Accountants and 4 Company Secretaries, in how many ways can a 5-member corporate audit committee be formed consisting of exactly 3 Chartered Accountants and 2 Company Secretaries?
explanation: Selecting 3 CAs out of 6 and 2 CSs out of 4 gives ⁶C₃ × ⁴C₂ = 20 × 6 = 120 committees.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 15: Permutations and Combinations

questionText: An economic research panel of 5 members is to be selected from 7 Economists and 5 Statisticians such that AT LEAST 3 Statisticians are included. How many distinct panels are possible?
explanation: Summing mutually exclusive cases: (3 Stat, 2 Econ) = ⁵C₃ × ⁷C₂ = 10 × 21 = 210; (4 Stat, 1 Econ) = ⁵C₄ × ⁷C₁ = 5 × 7 = 35; (5 Stat, 0 Econ) = ⁵C₅ × ⁷C₀ = 1. Total = 210 + 35 + 1 = 246.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 15: Permutations and Combinations

syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Probability

questionText: When two fair six-sided dice are rolled simultaneously, what is the probability of getting a sum of 9 on the upper faces?
explanation: Out of 36 equiprobable outcomes, sum = 9 occurs for {(3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3)} = 4 outcomes; probability = 4/36 = 1/9.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Probability

questionText: Two independent auditors A and B inspect a complex ledger; their individual probabilities of spotting a subtle posting error are 2/3 and 3/4 respectively. What is the probability that the error IS spotted (by at least one auditor)?
explanation: P(neither spots error) = (1 − 2/3)(1 − 3/4) = (1/3)(1/4) = 1/12. Hence P(at least one spots error) = 1 − 1/12 = 11/12.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Probability

questionText: At a commercial bank branch, 60% of customers hold Savings accounts, 40% hold Fixed Deposits, and 25% hold both. Given that a randomly chosen customer holds a Fixed Deposit, what is the conditional probability that she also holds a Savings account?

topic: Bayes' Theorem in Factory Quality Control
questionText: Machine M1 manufactures 60% of a plant's bolts with a 2% defective rate, while Machine M2 manufactures the remaining 40% with a 5% defective rate. A bolt drawn at random from combined output is found defective. What is the probability that it was produced by Machine M2?

questionText: A cabinet of 12 tax files contains 4 audited files and 8 unaudited files. If 3 files are selected at random without replacement, find the probability that AT LEAST ONE selected file is audited.
explanation: Total ways = ¹²C₃ = 220; ways with zero audited files (all 3 from 8 unaudited) = ⁸C₃ = 56. Thus P(at least 1 audited) = 1 − 56/220 = 1 − 14/55 = 41/55.

questionText: In the XY-coordinate plane, which region represents the solution set of the linear inequation 3x + 4y ≥ 12?

Closed half-plane bounded by 3x + 4y = 12 lying on the side NOT containing the origin (0, 0)
Open half-plane strictly excluding the boundary line 3x + 4y = 12

explanation: Testing origin (0, 0) in 3x + 4y ≥ 12 yields 0 ≥ 12 (False), and '≥' includes the boundary line; hence the solution is the closed non-origin side of 3x + 4y = 12.

questionText: A furniture workshop spends ₹500 on timber per chair (x) and ₹1,200 per table (y) within a weekly timber budget of at most ₹24,000, while storage holds at most 30 pieces in total. Which system of linear inequations models the feasible output?
explanation: 500x + 1,200y ≤ 24,000 simplifies (dividing by 100) to 5x + 12y ≤ 240, storage cap gives x + y ≤ 30, and non-negativity of physical output requires x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 17: Linear Inequations

topic: Corner Points and Maximum Profit Objective Over Feasible Polygon
questionText: Consider the bounded feasible region in the first quadrant defined by x + 2y ≤ 12, 2x + y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Find the interior intersection corner point of the two boundary lines and the maximum value of Z = 5x + 4y across the feasible region.
explanation: Solving x + 2y = 12 and 2x + y = 12 simultaneously gives x = 4, y = 4. Evaluating Z = 5x + 4y at all four corner points—(0, 0) → 0, (6, 0) → 30, (0, 6) → 24, and (4, 4) → 36—yields maximum Z = 36 at (4, 4).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 17: Linear Inequations

topic: Equivalent Single Discount for Successive Discounts
questionText: What single flat discount rate is equivalent to two successive trade discounts of 20% followed by 10%?
explanation: On ₹100 list price, 20% discount leaves ₹80, and a further 10% discount deducts ₹8 leaving ₹72 net—an equivalent single discount of 100 − 72 = 28%.

questionText: In commercial agency arithmetic, why is a 'Del Credere Agent' paid an extra Del Credere Commission over and above ordinary commission?

Because he pays the manufacturer's income tax out of pocket
Because he manufactures the raw materials himself
Because he sells goods strictly for cash without allowing credit

topic: Marked Price Setting for Target Profit After Discount
questionText: A trader buys an appliance for ₹1,800. What Marked Price (catalogue price) must he print on it so that after allowing a 10% discount on Marked Price, he still earns a 25% profit on Cost Price?
explanation: Target Selling Price = ₹1,800 × 1.25 = ₹2,250. Since Selling Price = 90% of Marked Price, MP = ₹2,250 ÷ 0.90 = ₹2,500.

topic: True Discount, Banker's Discount, and Banker's Gain
questionText: If the True Discount (TD) on a Bill of Exchange due 6 months hence at 10% p.a. simple interest is ₹2,400, compute the Face Value (Sum Due) of the bill, the Banker's Discount (BD), and the Banker's Gain (BG).

options.text: Face Value = ₹48,000, Banker's Discount = ₹2,400, and Banker's Gain = ₹120
Face Value = ₹50,400, Banker's Discount = ₹2,640, and Banker's Gain = ₹240
Face Value = ₹52,800, Banker's Discount = ₹2,520, and Banker's Gain = ₹120
Face Value = ₹50,400, Banker's Discount = ₹2,520, and Banker's Gain = ₹120

explanation: For 6 months @ 10% p.a., period rate = 5%. Since TD = 5% of Present Worth (PW) = ₹2,400, PW = ₹48,000 and Face Value = PW + TD = ₹50,400. Banker's Gain = 5% of TD = ₹120, and Banker's Discount = TD + BG = ₹2,520 (which equals 5% of ₹50,400).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 18: Commercial Arithmetic: Percentage, Profit & Brokerage
